newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian bond rally too sharp, seen reversing.
newsitem.headline: Indian bond rally too sharp, seen reversing.

text.p: A recent bull run in Indian government securities has driven prices sharply up but the rally may run out of steam soon, analysts and dealers said on Wednesday.
"I think the market is over-heated," said Aashish Pitale, debt research manager at ICICI Securities and Finance Company (I-Sec), the Indian affiliate of J.P. Morgan.
"Prices have been on the rise for quite some time now but the rise after the 11.83 percent 2003 bond auction has been particularly steep," Pitale said.

The central bank set a cut-off yield of 11.83 percent at an auction of six-year bonds on July 16, against market expectations of 11.90-11.95, triggering off a rally in which bonds of other tenures were repriced upwards.
"Yields jumped up by 30-50 basis points after the 11.83 percent bond auction," Pitale said. "This is very sharp."
Money market dealers agreed that a correction was due.
"Security prices have gone up on expectations of falling yields," said a dealer at a foreign bank. "I do not think people really expect a fall in general interest rates in the economy."
"But the easy liquidity with banks is being channelled into gilts, leading to a rise in prices (and a fall in yields)," he said. "Expectations are this will continue."
"This expectation is behind the current demand."
Bank investments in government securities have risen sharply on the back of strong deposit growth and poor demand for credit.
The latest Reserve Bank of India (RBI) figures show total bank deposits at 5,214.42 billion rupees on July 4, 1997, an increase of 775.89 billion over the year-ago figure.
Bank advances however grew by only 243.68 billion rupees in the same period, to 2,774.60 billion.
"Banks are investing in government securities because they cannot put their money elsewhere," the foreign bank dealer said.
But what is worrying analysts is that the increase in investments exceeds deposit growth.
Since the start of the current fiscal year on April 1, bank deposits grew 158.43 billion rupees but investment in government securities has risen 214 billion rupees, according to the RBI.

"This is going to create problems for banks when demand for credit picks up," said Pitale. "They will then be forced to unload securities in a hurry to raise cash and we will then see a crash in gilt prices."
Furthermore, he said at current prices, banks were possibly earning less than they were paying out.
"Most banks pay eight percent for a one-year deposit but the yield on a 364-day treasury bill is around 7.6-7.7 percent," Pitale added.
"Similarly the 10-year bond yields less than 12 percent while banks pay 12-13 percent for deposits above three years."
"This kind of mismatch cannot be sustained for long."
